name: Carla Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing gets traced back to you. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at four, because the bus to the pit leaves the town square at half five. I drive a haul truck at the Red Hill copper mine, one of the big ones, 220 tonnes when it's loaded. Twelve hours going round and round: under the shovel, up the ramp, tip at the crusher, back down. I like the quiet in the cab, honestly, but my eyes are gone by the end, and the dust gets in your teeth.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been driving?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years and a bit. Before that I did twenty-six years in the laundry at the district hospital, until they shipped the washing out to a contractor in the city and shut us down. The union got us a small payout and the mine was hiring, so here I am at fifty-eight, still the slowest on the ramp. My partner Tomas is a caretaker at the primary school, so between us we get by, just. There's not much saved, maybe three weeks if the truck broke down and so did we.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave us alone then. At the union meeting I'd probably say the hype was always about selling things to the bosses. I don't go online much, just the family group on my phone, and I wouldn't bother posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change much for me, because Red Hill was never waiting on clever computers. They've already got a trial in the north pit with six trucks that drive themselves, run off GPS and radar. The robots in the north pit don't need AI to be smart. They just need to be cheaper than me, and I'm not expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down, same as now. I'd go to every union meeting about the north pit trial, because that's the real fight whatever the computers do. Maybe I'd put an extra twenty a week aside, but that depends on the gas bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. But it's the kind of relief where you know the other problem is still sitting there in the north pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to the north pit. What do you actually see when you drive past it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You see the trucks with no one in them, just a blue light on top, going round like toy cars. Nobody waves. My friend Inés says it's eerie at night shift, because they keep moving when the rest of us are on break. I don't look too long, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the hype faded, would anything about your job get better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe they'd stop putting new screens in the cab every six months. I've only just learned the dispatch tablet and they keep changing the menus. If nothing changed for a while, I could finally get good at the job instead of always catching up.

S0.say: She'd tell the union meeting that the AI hype was always a sales pitch to bosses and that workers should be left alone. She doesn't post online and wouldn't start now.
S0.think: Privately she thinks AI hype barely matters to her, because the self-driving trucks already trialled in the north pit don't need clever AI. They only need to be cheaper than her, and she knows she isn't expensive.
S0.do: Keeps driving and keeps her head down. Goes to every union meeting about the self-driving truck trial, and tries to put aside an extra twenty a week if the gas bill allows.
S0.feel: Relieved, but only partly, because the robot trucks in the north pit are still there whatever happens to AI.
S0.quote: The robots in the north pit don't need AI to be smart. They just need to be cheaper than me, and I'm not expensive.
S0.fieldNote: Carla separates 'AI' from 'robots' more sharply than the card does: for her the threat is already parked in the north pit. Even the calm picture leaves her uneasy, because the trial trucks are real and she is the newest, slowest driver. Her small wish is telling: she wants the technology to stop changing long enough for her to get good at the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is what the union is for, and I'd want a deal in writing before one more truck goes driverless. To my sister I'd say the company will get richer and we'll get a leaflet about retraining. I'd sign any petition going around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, haul trucks are first in line. They've practically told us so with the north pit. If the company spreads that trial to the whole mine over a few years, the drivers with the least time go first, and that's me, two years in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask our delegate, Marco, what the agreement says about redundancy for people with short service, because I think it's next to nothing. We'd cut the car, Tomas can walk to the school, and stop helping our son with his rent. And I'd vote for whoever promises a law that says companies pay into a fund for every job they automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there'd be a leaflet about retraining. If the mine offered you a course to work the control room, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go, because you don't say no, but I'd be lying if I said I'd be good at it. I don't even use the self-checkout at the supermarket. Put me in front of six screens watching robots and I'll be the one who misses the alarm. The young ones would pick it up in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be thinking about at work if this started happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inés, mostly. She's a single mum and she's been driving here for eleven years, so she'd get a better payout than me, but she's got a girl at college. And old Pavel on the water cart, who's never done anything else. At least I've worked somewhere else before.

S1.say: She'd say this is exactly what the union is for and push for a written deal before any more trucks go driverless. She'd tell family the company will get richer while workers get a retraining leaflet.
S1.think: She believes haul trucks are first in line and that, as a driver with two years' service, she'd be among the first let go. She doubts she could cope with a control-room job watching robots.
S1.do: Asks the union delegate what short-service redundancy pay looks like and pushes for a fund paid by companies that automate. Sells the car and stops helping her son with his rent, and votes for candidates who back that fund.
S1.feel: Sick with dread, like waiting for a letter she knows is coming.
S1.quote: Put me in front of six screens watching robots and I'll be the one who misses the alarm.
S1.fieldNote: For Carla the 'mild' disruption is already a direct hit, because the first jobs to shrink look exactly like hers. Her answer is collective and political rather than personal; she doesn't picture herself retraining successfully and says so plainly. She is quick to think of colleagues worse off than her, which seems to steady her a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that the people who own these machines should pay for the people they replace. At the canteen I'd be loud about it. I'd probably even go on the marches if there were any, me and Tomas with a sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? I'd be finished, and fast. In two years I'm sixty, with no trade a robot can't do, three weeks of savings and no other mine within a day's drive. Twenty-six years of folding sheets and two years of driving, and none of it counts for anything a robot can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for every scrap of help the government offers, the day it's offered, no pride about it. We'd give up the car and the phone plans, and I'd go back to my sister's to save on rent if it came to that. And I'd stay in the union to fight for a decent payout, because that's the only money that would be coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I don't want to sound dramatic, but I'd be frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, is there anything you'd do differently in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. It's one more winter and some overtime. I'd take every extra shift going and put it in the jar, but I know that gets us maybe two months more, not two years. I wouldn't start a course; there's no time to finish one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas the night you heard it was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been poor before and we managed. He'd make tea and say something stupid to make me laugh, that's what he does. Then I'd lie awake and do the sums, because I'm the one who does the sums.

S2.say: She'd say loudly that the owners of the machines must pay for the people they replace, and she'd march with a sign if there were protests.
S2.think: She privately thinks she'd be finished within two years: sixty, no trade a robot can't do, three weeks of savings and no other mine nearby. She feels her whole working life would count for nothing.
S2.do: Applies for every form of government help as soon as it's offered and gives up the car and phone plans. Takes every overtime shift in the two years before, and stays in the union to fight for a payout.
S2.feel: Frightened, and a little embarrassed to say so.
S2.quote: Twenty-six years of folding sheets and two years of driving, and none of it counts for anything a robot can't do.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Carla stops talking about colleagues and talks about herself. Two years is not long enough to finish any course, so she doesn't even consider retraining; she reaches for overtime, the union and public help. She describes the night at home in detail, with Tomas making tea and her doing the sums, which says a lot about who carries the worry in that house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but with more time to organise. I'd tell people at work to get into the union now, while there's still a lot of us. Five years is enough time to make a real fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three when it hit. That's almost there but not quite, and the pension doesn't start for a few years after. Five years means I'd make it to the edge of retirement and then get pushed off the cliff before I reach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting a bit away every payday, even if it's just fifty, and I'd stop the lottery tickets. I'd go to the union every month and push them to bargain for early pensions for the over-sixties. And I'd write to our member of parliament, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Less scared than with two years, but more like a long, slow worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd write to your MP. What would the letter say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people like me didn't choose this, and we shouldn't have to beg. That if a company saves millions on drivers, a slice of it should bridge us to the pension. I'd probably ask my daughter to help with the spelling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about learning the new systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. If there's time, maybe I'd try the control room course, just so I'm not the first name on the list. But I'm not going to pretend I'd enjoy it. I'd do it the way you take medicine.

S3.say: She'd tell co-workers to join the union now, while there are still many of them, and use the five years to organise.
S3.think: She thinks five years would take her right to the edge of retirement and then push her off before her pension starts, at sixty-three.
S3.do: Saves around fifty each payday and stops buying lottery tickets. Pushes the union to bargain for early pensions for the over-sixties and writes to her MP for the first time, perhaps reluctantly trying the control room course.
S3.feel: A long, slow tightness rather than outright fear.
S3.quote: Five years means I'd make it to the edge of retirement and then get pushed off the cliff before I reach it.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years buy her an organising window, and she uses it for collective action and politics rather than personal reinvention. She'd consider the control-room course only as defence, 'like medicine', which fits her resistance to new technology. The gap between sixty-three and the pension is the detail that keeps her mood high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the young ones who need protecting now, not me. At the meetings I'd be the old lady telling them to sign up for every course while it's free. Online I'd still say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight. If I keep my head down and they keep a few drivers on, I might just make it to the pension. Ten years is the first one where I can picture my last shift happening on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and pray the trial stays a trial for a while. I'd try to save a little every month and get the car paid off. And I'd keep pushing the union, but more for Inés's girl and the young drivers than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. Not happy, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'pray the trial stays a trial'. Is that hope, or a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hope, mostly. My plan is the same as ever: show up, don't crash, keep my head down. The truth is I'm not the type to jump before I'm pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your grandchildren to know about how you got through it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That their nan wasn't clever with machines, but she stuck with her people. That the union is the reason any of us got anything. I'd want them to know you don't get through these things alone.

S4.say: She'd say the young workers need protecting now, and urge them to take every free course while it lasts.
S4.think: She thinks she might just reach her pension at sixty-eight if a few drivers are kept on, and for the first time she can picture finishing on her own terms.
S4.do: Keeps driving and pays off the car, saving a little each month. Keeps pushing the union, mainly on behalf of younger drivers.
S4.feel: Easier and able to breathe, though not happy.
S4.quote: Ten years is the first one where I can picture my last shift happening on my own terms.
S4.fieldNote: Carla is clearest about time here: ten years carries her to sixty-eight, past the gap that scared her in the faster pictures. Her plan is still mostly hope and staying put, which she admits openly. She sees herself through the union, and wants her grandchildren to remember that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. What would help is a bridge to the pension for people over fifty-five, paid for by the companies that bring in the robot trucks, and a union strong enough to make them pay it. Not a course, a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women. There are eleven of us on trucks at Red Hill, and most of us came late, after the kids or after some other job closed. They hired us because the trucks are easy to drive now, and they'll fire us because the trucks are easy to drive now.

headlineQuote: They hired us because the trucks are easy to drive now, and they'll fire us because the trucks are easy to drive now.
portrait: Carla Alvarez is 58 and drives a 220-tonne haul truck at the Red Hill copper mine, a job she took two years ago after the hospital laundry where she worked for twenty-six years was outsourced. She has about three weeks of savings, a partner who is a school caretaker, and no other mine nearby. She sees the self-driving trucks already on trial in the north pit as the real threat, whatever happens to AI, so she is uneasy even in the calm picture and alarmed in the faster ones. Her answers turn to the union, public help and a pension bridge rather than retraining, which she doubts she could manage. Only the ten-year picture lets her imagine reaching her pension on her own terms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because at sixty she'd lose her job with no trade a robot can't do, almost no savings and no other mine nearby.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge to the pension for workers over fifty-five, paid for by the companies that bring in robot trucks, and a union strong enough to win it.
